analysis.one_liner: Caps bank overdraft fees at one per month and bans fees on declined ATM and debit transactions.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 46 Democratic cosponsors in March 2013, the bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the rules banks follow when a customer spends more money than is in their checking account. It would cap overdraft fees at one per month and six per year per account, require fees to be proportional to the amount overdrawn, ban fees outright on declined ATM and debit card transactions, and require banks to disclose the fee as an annual percentage rate so customers can compare it to other credit. It never got a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who overdraw their checking accounts — disproportionately low- and moderate-income households, per the bill's own findings — who currently pay flat fees of around $30 or more each time the bank covers a shortfall, sometimes several in a single day.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low- and moderate-income checking account holders

how_it_helps.text: Caps overdraft coverage fees at no more than one per calendar month and six per calendar year per account, and requires any fee to be reasonable and proportional to the amount overdrawn.
Prohibits banks from charging a nonsufficient funds fee on any ATM or debit card transaction — the fee charged when the bank declines a payment instead of covering it.

Requires banks to disclose the overdraft fee as an annual percentage rate so consumers can meaningfully compare it to alternatives like linked accounts or credit lines, and to disclose that if they do not opt in, a transaction may be declined but no fee is charged.
Bans overdraft fees when the overdraft results solely from a debit hold larger than the actual transaction, and bars fee increases during a one-year moratorium after enactment.
Requires prompt same-day notification when overdraft coverage is used, with the fee amount and the balance needed to restore the account.

analysis.who_pays: Banks and credit unions, which collect billions of dollars a year in overdraft and nonsufficient funds fees; the bill's own findings state that these fees fall hardest on low- and moderate-income consumers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Banks and credit unions collecting overdraft fees

drawbacks.text: Banks keep discretion to reject overdrafts beyond the capped numbers without charging a fee, meaning some consumers could have transactions declined at the register rather than covered.

Some consumers use overdraft coverage as short-term emergency credit; the bill's caps and marketing restrictions could reduce that availability, and banks might offset lost fee income through other account charges or terms.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the households the bill's findings identify as bearing 'significant financial burdens' — those hit with repeated flat fees on small transactions — the caps and disclosure rules would be a clear gain, and requiring the fee to be shown as an APR exposes how expensive the credit actually is. The main cost falls on the banks' fee revenue, and the main risk to consumers is that banks respond by declining transactions or repricing other services rather than absorbing the loss.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Carolyn Maloney introduced the Overdraft Protection Act of 2013 on March 19, 2013, with 43 original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day, the only committee action ever recorded.
It gathered 46 cosponsors, all Democrats, over the course of the Congress.
No further action was taken through the end of the 113th Congress on January 3, 2015, so the bill died in committee without a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and credit unions came out ahead: because the bill never advanced, they kept charging overdraft and nonsufficient funds fees under the existing rules, which the bill's findings described as imposing significant burdens on low- and moderate-income consumers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Banks that collect overdraft fee revenue

sides.party_line_note: All 46 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the Republican-controlled Financial Services Committee took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would cap overdraft fees at six per year per account, require them to be proportional to the overdraft, and ban nonsufficient funds fees on ATM and debit transactions — a direct cut into fee income that the bill's findings say comes disproportionately from low- and moderate-income customers. The bill never advanced, so banks kept the existing fee structure.

The bill directs the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to study prepaid card overdraft practices and, if abusive practices are found, apply the same fee limits to prepaid cards. This risked extending the crackdown beyond traditional bank accounts.
